thread.title: Qualcomm and 2 Other Safe, High-Yield Stocks

author: Lawrence C. Strauss
title: Qualcomm and 2 Other Safe, High-Yield Stocks
text:
Photo: Kyle Dorosz By Lawrence C. Strauss June 6, 2018 12:42 p.m. ET The S&P 500 yields about 2%. That’s not nearly enough for Jenny Van Leeuwen Harrington, a portfolio manager and CEO of Gilman Hill Asset Management. A value investor who likes to pore over a firm’s financials, Harrington looks for beaten-down names across the market-capitalization spectrum. In some cases, Harrington can find better yields—around 3% to 4%—among well-known companies like Target or Qualcomm .
To her, a company’s dividend should be sacrosanct, even in tough economic times. Because of her value-bent, the strategy, which is available in separate accounts, has lagged the S&P 500 over various periods. But the portfolio’s composite has lost money in only two calendar years since 2007—one of them was 2008, when it lost 30%, versus a 37% decline for the benchmark. Since its inception in October of 2006, the strategy’s composite has a net annual return of 6.35%, two percentage points behind the S&P 500, as of April 30.
Barron’s sat down with Harrington, 42, recently to hear more about her investing approach and some of her holdings. The New Canaan, Conn., firm oversees about $355 million, of which $147 million is in equity-income stocks.
Barron’s : How would you sum up your investing approach?
Van Leeuwen Harrington: The people whose portfolios I manage have worked to save every penny. They are mostly retired, and they are investing in this dividend-income strategy because that’s the income they need to live on. The primary approach I take is to look at a company and know that its dividends are safe, come hell or high water, and that we could go through the worst of times, like 2008-2009, and there should be no interruption to those dividends. I’m looking for a resilient stream of cash flows that support the dividends that’s almost tangible—that you can really see and feel and sink your teeth into.
Why do you benchmark the equity-income strategy against the S&P 500, and have you thought about changing your benchmark?
This is an absolute-return strategy. The objective is to generate 5% or better dividend income, and have growth on top of that. With every stock I buy, my objective is to have a minimum annual return of 8%-10% over the long run. We’re putting the S&P down as a benchmark because there is nothing that is actually a good effective benchmark for this strategy. We’ve toyed with creating an internal one where we would have a weighting of, say, 15% master limited partnerships, 20% real estate investment trusts, 10% utilities, and the balance in the S&P 500. But even that’s not really that genuine. So we think it is better for people to be able to make their own decision on the benchmark.
How has the big thirst for income—and how investors have bid up the price of certain sectors that act like bond proxies such as utilities—impacted the types of stocks you can find?
It’s not much harder to find high-dividend stocks today than it was when I started this strategy more than a decade ago. I’m an all-cap manager with a value approach, and there is always something that has fallen out of favor. Also, my biggest competitors tend to have multibillions in assets under management, so they can’t invest in the smaller-cap companies the way I can. You can find things that have just slipped or that don’t necessarily fall into traditional value and dividend-yield screens. Who knew, for example, that Target (ticker: TGT), which I added to the portfolio last year, would ever be something that I could invest in?
Value stocks have lagged growth names for many years. How has that impacted your performance and stock-picking?
Last year was hell with respect to relative performance, and heaven with respect to what I was able to invest in. In 2017 I was able to add Seagate Technology (STX), CenturyLink (CTL), Target, Navient (NAVI), Tanger Factory Outlet Centers (SKT), Pitney Bowes (PBI), and Owens & Minor (OMI). The biggest multiple on any of these at the time was 12 times forward earnings, and all of them had yields of at least 4½% when we initiated these positions. These were collectively once-in-a-lifetime kinds of bargains, and they were a direct result of the lack of love for value or just anything without significant growth. Right now the portfolio’s yield is 5.7%, which is nuts. So with respect to meeting that objective of a 5% yield or better, I have never had an easier time finding those opportunities.
What are a few examples of stocks you hold and how they reflect your stock-picking style?
Six Flags Entertainment (SIX) is super-interesting in that it has an incredibly high barrier to entry. You can’t just start a new theme park. The other thing—and this is from the beginning and it remains true today—is there is a huge degree of economic insensitivity with this company. When the economy does turn down, you see their revenues stay very stable because of the “staycation” concept. People might cancel their big trip to Disney , but then they go to the local Six Flags instead. That’s something that initially caught my attention. Six Flags filed for bankruptcy protection in 2009, and a new management team emerged after that. That team has been unbelievable in its consistency. For example, every year they consistently raise the cost of their season pass. It is pennies to the consumer, but it is significant to the bottom line. They’ve cut their operating costs dramatically. Tax reform was good for them. It has added roughly $40 million to their bottom line.
They have steadily been growing their adjusted Ebitda [earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization]. As of the first quarter, it totaled $574 million over the previous 12 months, compared with $520 million in 2015. The quarterly dividend has grown since 2013 from 45 cents a share to 78 cents most recently. They are completely committed to the dividend, and they have really significant growth plans between now and 2020. The company aims to reach $750 million in adjusted Ebitda by 2020, which would be 10% annualized growth between 2017 and 2020. They are doing international licenses in countries such as Dubai, China, and Saudi Arabia. Plus, you get around a 5% dividend yield. In the worst case, you are getting that yield and probably a minimum of 5% capital appreciation per year between now and 2020.
Even if the multiple doesn’t expand?
Yes, you don’t even need multiple expansion on the stock. Conservatively, you can make the case for a 10% total return per year over the next two years.
Let’s move on to another holding, preferably in a different sector.
By a huge margin, L Brands (LB), whose brands include Victoria’s Secret, is the market leader in the bra and intimate apparel segment. Its appeal cuts across socioeconomic segments, whether it’s Fairfield County in Connecticut or parts of Appalachia, an observation I picked up recently from reading the book Hillbilly Elegy . Many retailing stocks have seen significant declines over the past few years. We had to pick through and look at Barnes & Noble (BKS), Abercrombie & Fitch (ANF), GameStop (GME), and Macy’s (M), among others, and figure out their values. For some of them, the big stock declines are justified. But we found that L Brands’ combination of cash-flow resilience and dividend coverage was the most compelling of the retailers we looked at.
L Brands has an estimated dividend this fiscal year, which ends in January, of about $2.40 a share. The stock trades at 12.7 times my expected earnings of $2.90 a share. But it’s yielding 6.5%. By any measure, this company has an excellent management team that knows how to weather economic cycles. Revenues were flattish in its most recent fiscal year, but they are still up about 20% from where they were five years ago.
How much upside is there?
You could easily have more than a 10% return over the next year if you got just one point of multiple expansion to nearly 14 times, based on sentiment turning around. I don’t even need this company to earn more. Let’s say earnings stay stable at $2.90 a share, and you have one multiple point of expansion. That’s nearly a $40 stock, compared with around $37 recently. Plus, you add on the 6.5% dividend yield, which is really significant. But realistically you could see a multiple of 14 times.
Doesn’t the company have to improve its revenue growth?
I don’t think so. I do believe there is earnings growth ahead of it. Even if it is 3% to 4% growth, when you have a stock that is down more than 20% over the past year and is being treated like it is dead, the earnings are not down 50%. There is a disconnect there, however, and the market threw out that whole sector. Not too long ago the stock was trading at 15 times. So it is hard to say exactly what the right multiple is. But I do know that 12.7 times is not the right multiple, and I expect they will earn $2.90 this year, $3.02 the following year, and maybe $3.14 the year after that. There is no carnage ahead in earnings expectations.
How about another sector?
Qualcomm (QCOM) has a 4.2% yield and a market capitalization of about $88 billion. In its previous fiscal year, which ended last September, it earned $4.28 a share and paid a dividend of $2.20. Analyst estimates are all over the map, but call it about $3.50 of earnings in the current fiscal year. You still have a dividend that is very well covered. Management opposed having the company acquired by Broadcom (AVGO), a deal that didn’t go through.
Newsletter Sign-up In early March, when Broadcom was still pursuing Qualcomm, the company put out a press release in which it said there was “a clear and achievable path toward” non-GAAP earnings of $6.75 to $7.50 a share in fiscal 2019. So if that’s right, you have got a stock that is trading at eight times the low end of their range. The investment community barely blinked at that guidance. I don’t know if that’s because they completely dismissed it or there was just so much noise.
What makes their business attractive?
Qualcomm is responsible for the majority of chips being used in the majority of cellphones. The stock is controversial for several reasons. Qualcomm and Apple (AAPL) are involved in lawsuits over the licensing of chips used in iPhones and iPads. Another source of controversy is Qualcomm’s attempt to acquire NXP Semiconductors (NXPI), a deal that’s become mired in trade-war concerns with China. And then there was the Broadcom takeover attempt. One other piece of the story: Paul Jacobs, the son of the company’s co-founder, mounted a bid in the spring to acquire the company.
There has been a lot of noise around this stock, and that’s kept a significant lid on the valuation. Don’t forget that they make an essential product that’s needed for the transition to faster 5G wireless technology. It’s the Snapdragon 5G Module Solutions, which helps equipment suppliers make smartphones that are 5G compatible.
Qualcomm’s stock really hasn’t done much over the past year, with a flattish return. What else do you like about it?
Last month, the company announced a new share-buyback program for up to $10 billion. That’s a lot of money, more than 10% of its market cap. So even if we are wrong and earnings are only $4.50 a share in 2019 and you have a 13½ multiple, that would be a $61 stock. If management’s projections are right and the company earns $6.75 a share in fiscal 2019, you could have a $91 stock using the same multiple.
What’s the catalyst for this stock?
Increasing transparency.
In what way?
The termination of the Broadcom deal is one factor, and the NXP merger is more likely to happen as the trade rhetoric with China cools. I expect this management buyout effort to subside, and there will be less noise around the stock.
Thanks, Jenny.
